ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: A certain laboratory keeps wild-type and some mutant fruit flies. Some recessive mutant genes of fruit flies and their positions on chromosomes are shown in the figure. Answer the question: Student B crossed singed-bristle white-eye male flies with wild-type (straight-bristle red-eye) homozygous female flies (forward cross). Then what is the probability that singed-bristle individuals appear among the male offspring?

ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: A certain laboratory keeps wild-type and some mutant fruit flies. Some recessive mutant genes of fruit flies and their positions on chromosomes are shown in the figure. Answer the question: Student B crossed singed-bristle white-eye male flies with wild-type (straight-bristle red-eye) homozygous female flies (forward cross). Then what is the probability that singed-bristle individuals appear among the male offspring?
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: The image shows the positions of some recessive mutant genes of fruit flies on chromosomes: on the X chromosome are marked w white eye and sn singed bristle; on chromosome No. 2 are dp outstretched wing and pr purple eye; on chromosome No. 3 are ru rough eye and e ebony body. From the figure, it can be known that white eye w and singed bristle sn are both located on the X chromosome. The stem states that these mutant genes are recessive. The forward cross carried out by Student B is: singed-bristle white-eye male fly × wild-type homozygous female fly. It can be denoted as male fly X^(w sn)Y, female fly X^(+ +)X^(+ +). The Y chromosome of male fruit fly offspring comes from the father, and the only X chromosome comes from the mother; while the mother is wild-type homozygous and can only provide X^(+ +). Therefore, all male offspring have wild-type alleles at the sn locus and will not show the recessive singed-bristle trait, so the probability that singed-bristle individuals appear among the male offspring is 0.
